claims.text: The bad-question example in that file is the single sentence 'Viết cho tôi chức năng hủy đơn hàng', and the file gives its cost as code that looks reasonable, uses a library you do not have, and follows conventions that are not the team's.

The good-question example in the same file attaches the code (OrderService.Cancel, marked '(dán code)'), the versions (.NET 10 and PostgreSQL 17), the business rule, the current wrong behaviour, and one constraint ('Đừng viết lại cả phương thức'), and asks for reasoning plus the platform cause.
The versions named in that file, .NET 10 and PostgreSQL 17, are the versions pinned in content/versions.yaml for the keys dotnet and postgresql.

The same file's 'Ba việc nên giao' lists exactly three: explaining unfamiliar code, generating test cases (listing edge cases for a method), and rubber-ducking (writing the problem out for a machine to read, where you often see the bug yourself).

The same file's 'Ba việc không nên giao' lists exactly three: questions about default values, limits and versions; code you have not read line by line; and real customer data, which must not be pasted into any outside tool.

The same file states as its reason for sending version and default questions to the documentation that the assistant produces text that sounds reasonable, not verified truth ('không phải sự thật đã kiểm chứng').

The same file's closing paragraph compares the assistant to a very confident, broadly informed colleague who is sometimes completely wrong in the same voice used when right, and prescribes treating its output as that colleague's draft: read, check, then use.
The same file states 'Bạn ký tên vào commit, không phải nó' — the commit carries your name, not the assistant's.

A prompt carrying five parts — the code, the versions in force, the rule that must hold, what happens instead, one constraint — yields an answer you can judge; three words and a file do not, because nothing says what would count as wrong. The parts are named in full in sections 3, 4 and the summary.
A reply of 'still wrong' carries no new information, so it gives the assistant nothing new to work from and the next version is another guess; the step that helps is a changed prompt.
Asking for the reasoning and for a place in the documentation gives the answer its own handle for checking; an answer with no stated basis can only be accepted or rejected whole.

Work worth handing over is work whose result you can check cheaply — a run, or a list you only have to read and prune — which is why a wrong list of edge cases is still useful and a wrong default value is not. The lesson adds repetitive code a single run settles, beyond the page's three.

Writing the failure out for a machine to read often shows you the bug before any answer arrives, so the writing is worth doing even unsent; the lesson attributes this to the file's 'Vịt cao su' item, which says you frequently see the error yourself.
A confident tone is not evidence that anything was checked: a wrong answer and a correct one arrive worded alike, which is why an apology followed by an equally certain third version is the symptom.

The person named on a commit answers for every line in it, whatever produced them, because someone on the team reads the change before it is merged, and the code is later read and changed by people who ask why it is written that way.

Nothing in the situation's prompt said which project it was for, and what came back showed it: a naming style this repository does not use and a helper method it does not have. Stated as what the answer showed, not as the cause of it.
The page's bad question has the same shape as the situation's prompt — a line of intent and nothing else — but a different subject: it asks for an order-cancel feature, not a fix to a wrong total.
An edge case is an unusual input at the boundary of what a method accepts.

A test is a small run that calls a method on chosen inputs and checks what comes back.
